business_problem: Microsoft's quantum program had to improve qubit reliability and speed while coordinating software, architecture, materials, fabrication, and measurement work across large, siloed datasets and globally distributed specialists. Manual experimentation and measurement cycles took weeks, complex parameter tuning was hard to scale, and hidden fabrication issues were difficult to detect quickly.
solution_summary: Microsoft used Microsoft Discovery's agentic AI capabilities inside its quantum R&D workflow to support the Majorana 2 program. The platform lets the team deploy AI agents, guided by scientists, to reason over nearly two decades of heterogeneous project data spanning software, device architecture, materials, fabrication processes, and measurements. In practice, agents manage workflows, synthesize cross-disciplinary knowledge, correlate data trapped in silos, and recommend likely experimental targets before physical testing. The team also built specialized agents to automate qubit-state measurement, perform parallel voltage adjustments, and generate 3D maps of operating conditions that would be impractical for a single researcher. Additional agents filtered fabrication data and identified anomalies such as a miscalibrated temperature sensor. Outputs are served back to scientists in a human-in-the-loop process that informs materials choices, fabrication optimization, experiment design, and root-cause analysis for device reliability.

solution_components.name: Microsoft Discovery
solution_components.role: Provides the agentic AI platform the quantum team uses to manage workflows, synthesize siloed data, automate measurements, optimize fabrication, and generate recommendations for scientists.

data_flow: Historical quantum project data from software, architecture, materials, fabrication, and measurement systems is analyzed in Microsoft Discovery by specialized AI agents. The agents correlate siloed information, run simulations, automate measurement and voltage-adjustment loops, build 3D operating maps, and flag anomalies; their recommendations are then reviewed by scientists and fed back into device design, fabrication, and experiment execution.
